blocks.x: Fall has officially entered New York City—but it didn’t come alone.

Meteorologists are tracking a rare September nor’easter that could bring several days of rain, powerful winds, coastal flooding, high surf, and beach erosion to the East Coast later this week and into the weekend.
And yes, New York City could feel the effects.

The storm is still developing, and there’s significant uncertainty around exactly how strong it will become and how close it will track to the coast. But current forecasts show the potential for a potent coastal storm to develop off the Mid-Atlantic and move toward the Northeast, with the NYC area potentially seeing periods of heavy rain and gusty winds.
According to AccuWeather, the storm could even take on some characteristics of a tropical storm if it strengthens and lingers offshore.
So, what exactly is happening with this storm?
The setup is a little complicated—but the short version is that a storm system is expected to develop along the East Coast as a dip in the jet stream becomes more pronounced.
AccuWeather Senior Meteorologist Chad Merrill said that as this dip develops, a new storm could form along the coast or as far as a couple hundred miles offshore.
And where that storm ultimately tracks will make a huge difference for New York City.
If the storm stays farther offshore and remains weaker, NYC could see a relatively manageable round of rain and wind.
But if it strengthens over the ocean and tracks closer to the coast, the region could be dealing with stronger winds, heavier rain, higher surf and coastal flooding.
That’s why meteorologists are still watching this one closely.

Shutterstock / Colin Dewar
NYC could see days of rain and gusty winds
For New Yorkers, the biggest concerns right now are rain, wind, and potential flooding, rather than snow.
NBC 4 reports that if the storm deepens and passes just offshore, rainfall could exceed 3 to 4 inches in parts of Long Island, with lower amounts farther east from the storm’s center.
The NYC area could also experience gusty northeast winds, particularly if the coastal low strengthens and moves closer to shore.

The Weather Channel is also warning that several inches of rain could fall across parts of the region, potentially creating travel disruptions and flash-flooding concerns if heavier bands of rain set up along the coast.
And while NYC itself may not see the strongest winds in every forecast scenario, Long Island and the Connecticut coast could be much windier if the storm takes a closer track.
NBC 4 says a worst-case scenario could bring wind gusts exceeding 50 mph on eastern Long Island and the Connecticut coast.

Shutterstock / Donald Bowers Photography
Coastal flooding and beach erosion are also concerns
The storm’s biggest impacts may be felt along the coast.
A strong northeast wind blowing toward the shoreline can push ocean water inland, creating coastal flooding and causing waves to pound beaches and shorelines.

AccuWeather says coastal flooding is already possible from North Carolina to Massachusetts this week, with the threat potentially continuing along the northern Mid-Atlantic and expanding into southeastern New England over the weekend.
The NYC area’s coastline—including parts of Brooklyn, Queens, and Staten Island—could therefore see elevated water levels if the storm tracks close enough to the region.
Long Island and the Jersey Shore could also experience high surf and beach erosion.
There’s another factor that could make coastal flooding worse: the full moon.
AccuWeather notes that astronomical tide levels will be elevated later this week, meaning the storm could push water levels even higher around high tide.
Could this actually become a tropical storm?
Potentially—but don’t start calling it a tropical storm just yet.
Meteorologists say the system could develop tropical or subtropical characteristics if it strengthens while lingering over the Atlantic.
AccuWeather notes that the storm could potentially be classified as a hybrid or subtropical storm this weekend depending on how it develops.
That doesn’t mean a hurricane is headed for NYC. The current forecast is for a nor’easter/coastal storm, and the exact strength and track remain uncertain.

Pexels / Jesse R
The forecast could still change
This is probably the most important thing to know right now: we don’t have the final forecast yet.
As of Monday, NBC 4 noted that the low-pressure system had not even fully developed, and weather models were showing significant differences in both the storm’s strength and track.
The European model has been showing a stronger storm that tracks relatively close to the East Coast, which would mean more rain, stronger winds, higher surf and greater coastal impacts.
The American GFS model has been keeping the storm weaker and farther offshore, which would result in less significant impacts.
Those models will continue to change as the storm develops.
So while NYC could be in for a very wet and windy end to the week, it’s too early to say exactly how severe conditions will be in the city.
For now, meteorologists are watching the storm’s track closely. And if it strengthens and turns toward the coast, New Yorkers could be looking at a very soggy start to fall.
